explanation: Removing +sizeof("") (which is 1) means the allocation is one byte too short, so the null terminator written by memcpy overflows the buffer by one byte.
Removing the +1 for null terminator in ensure() means the printbuffer is allocated one byte too small, causing a one-byte overflow when the null terminator is written.
Removing +1 from allocation means the null terminator write at number_c_string[number_string_length] goes one byte past the allocation.

can_access_at_index(buffer, 4) checks that offset+4 < length (i.e. at least 5 bytes). Changing to index 3 allows BOM detection on a 4-byte input. After skipping 3 bytes, offset=3, and subsequent parsing reads past the end of a 3-byte BOM-only input.

Changing skipped_bytes from size_t to int causes silent truncation when a string has more than INT_MAX escape sequences, making allocation_length too large or wrapping negative, leading to under-allocation and subsequent heap overflow.
Removing the local null-assignment after free in cJSON_free; minimal impact since it's a local copy, not a strong site.

Off-by-one: allocation is 1 byte short. The buffer needs space for '/' prefix + encoded key + target_pointer + NUL. With +1 instead of +2 the NUL terminator written by encode_string_as_pointer/strcat overflows by 1 byte. Keys containing '~' or '/' double-encode and make the encoded length larger than the raw key, worsening the overflow.

sizeof("/") is 2 (the '/' character plus NUL). Removing it means the allocation is 2 bytes too small. The sprintf writes a '/' separator and encode_string_as_pointer writes the NUL terminator past the end of the allocation. Triggered whenever compose_patch is called with a non-NULL suffix (e.g. during create_patches on an object or array).

The original code for ~1 mistakenly writes to decoded_string[1] instead of decoded_string[0], leaving garbage in the decoded output. This is a latent logic bug; when combined with the advance of string++ the decoded pointer diverges, potentially writing a '/' one byte ahead of where the decoder cursor sits, corrupting adjacent memory in the decoded string buffer.

sizeof("/") is 2 (char + NUL). Using +1 instead allocates one byte too few. The sprintf writes path + '/' and encode_string_as_pointer writes the encoded key plus NUL terminator, overflowing the buffer by 1 byte. Triggered when cJSONUtils_GeneratePatches compares two objects with matching keys.
Shrinks the allocation by 1 extra byte in parse_string, so output_pointer writes past the allocated buffer when copying string content
Underestimates output_length in print_string_ptr by 1 when escape_characters>0, causing writes past the end of the allocated buffer

Off-by-one in overflow guard: when needed==INT_MAX exactly, the check incorrectly returns NULL blocking a valid allocation, but more critically the follow-up needed*2 path can overflow for inputs just below INT_MAX

can_read checks offset+size <= length (allows i==length-offset), while can_access_at_index checks offset+index < length. Switching to can_read allows one extra loop iteration, reading one byte past the buffer
Off-by-one in surrogate pair boundary check allows reading one byte past the input end when processing the second UTF-16 sequence
Off-by-one weakens the boundary check for the first UTF-16 sequence, allowing parse_hex4 to read one byte past a near-end-of-buffer escape sequence
Changing the overflow guard from INT_MAX to INT_MAX+1 allows 'needed' to equal INT_MAX+1 without triggering the guard, causing integer overflow in size calculation and under-allocation.
Changing i < 4 to i <= 4 causes parse_hex4 to read 5 characters instead of 4, reading one byte past the end of a \uXXXX sequence, potentially going out of bounds.
Removing the +1 from the allocation for number_c_string means the null terminator written at number_c_string[number_string_length] is one byte past the allocation, causing a heap-buffer-overflow.
Since utf8_position is an unsigned char, changing > 0 to >= 0 creates an infinite loop (unsigned char wraps from 0 to 255), writing far beyond the output buffer causing heap corruption
Adding 8 to the memcpy length in cJSON_strdup causes it to read 8 bytes past the source string and write 8 bytes past the allocated buffer.
Halving the allocation in parse_string means the output buffer is roughly half the size needed. The string copy loop writes past the end of the buffer.
Halving the allocation for number_c_string means the memcpy of the full number string overflows the buffer by roughly half the string length.
Adding 8 to the memcpy length in print_string_ptr (no-escape path) reads 8 bytes past the input string and writes 8 bytes past the ensure'd output buffer.

explanation: Removing sizeof("") (which is 1) from cJSON_strdup length calculation. Buffer is 1 byte too small and memcpy writes the NUL terminator past the allocation.
Removing the bounds check in parse_string allows input_end to walk past the end of the input buffer while scanning for the closing quote, causing heap-buffer-overflow read.
Adding 16 to the memcpy length for number string causes reading 16 bytes past the number in the input buffer and writing past the allocated number_c_string.
A vulnerability exists in the buffer access boundary check macro where a comparison operator allows reading one byte past the allocated input buffer.
A vulnerability exists in the string scanning loop where the boundary check allows iteration one byte past the input buffer when the closing quote is missing.
Off-by-one in string scanning loop allows reading one byte past input buffer while searching for closing quote
Heap overflow in parse_string: string allocation doubly subtracts escape byte count
Heap overflow in print_string_ptr: escape character count for control chars underestimated by 2 per char
Heap overflow in cJSON_strdup: allocation one byte short, memcpy writes past buffer
A vulnerability exists in the internal cJSON node constructor where the allocation is undersized, causing subsequent initialization to overflow the heap buffer.
A vulnerability exists in the internal string duplication function where the destination buffer is allocated at half the required size.
A vulnerability exists in the internal node constructor where the zero-initialization writes past the allocated memory region.
